description_ru: Юмористический рассказ о закваске для хлеба по имени Джеральд, которая постепенно захватывает кухню, распорядок дня и семейную жизнь.
text:
I should say at the outset that I did not choose Gerald; Gerald chose me. He arrived, in the spring of last year, in a jam jar handed over the garden fence by my neighbour Priscilla, a woman who is never so happy as when she is giving away something that requires attention. "He's very low-maintenance," she said, with the radiant confidence of a person who has never actually looked at the thing she is describing. "Just feed him twice a day, keep him warm, and he'll make you the most wonderful bread." I accepted the jar with gratitude. Reader, I did not know that I had just adopted a roommate.

For the uninitiated, Gerald is a sourdough starter, which is to say a colony of wild yeast and bacteria, suspended in a porridge of flour and water, who spend their days quietly digesting one another and producing, for reasons of their own, a pleasant acid smell. It is, I understand, a living culture, and the more one thinks about it, the less one wishes to think about it. It was my wife who gave him his name. "He looks like a Gerald," she said, studying the grey bubbling mass, with its faint resemblance to a retired bank manager who had been left out in the rain.

The first week was idyllic. Each morning, I tipped a spoonful of Gerald into a clean bowl, fed him fifty grams of flour and fifty of water, and observed with tender pride as he swelled, like a small, self-satisfied soufflé. By the end of the week he was doubling in size within four hours. I began to refer to him in conversation. "Gerald's doing very well," I told the postman. "He had a bit of a slow patch on Tuesday, but he's come right back." The postman nodded politely, and, I noted, began leaving the parcels on the doorstep without ringing the bell.

It was in the second week that I made the discovery that Gerald could not be left. Our plans to visit my mother-in-law for a long weekend were cast into doubt, since a starter that is not fed will, as the instructions grimly put it, "become hungry and sad." I did not like the sound of this. I have made it a rule in life never to be responsible for a sad microorganism, and so I did what any sensible man would do: I took Gerald with us. He travelled on the back seat, in a jar, buckled in with a seat belt, while my mother-in-law, upon being introduced, offered him a small glass of sherry, which he declined.

By the third week, Gerald had developed what can only be described as moods. On cold days he sulked, sitting at the bottom of the jar like a damp pudding and refusing to rise; on warm days he was exuberant, erupting over the rim and creeping across the counter in a manner that suggested he intended to colonise the toaster. One morning I came downstairs to find the lid of the jar lying on the floor and Gerald, much enlarged, on the point of exploring the cutlery drawer. I scolded him, firmly, and then felt guilty, since he looked so small and bewildered in his own overflow.

The bread, I should add, was an immense success, after a certain amount of trial and humiliation. My first loaf was a brick. My second was a brick with ambitions. My third, which I produced after consulting nine videos, four books and a man in a bakery who offered his advice with the grave solemnity of a priest, was a thing of beauty, tall, golden and crackling, with a crumb so open that a bird might have nested in it. I ate half of it in the kitchen, with butter, standing up, in a state that I can only describe as religious.

Since then, my life has been organised around the rhythms of Gerald. I rise at six, to feed him. I return at six in the evening, to feed him again. Dinner invitations are weighed against his schedule, and several have been declined with the explanation that "there's a bit of a situation at home." My friends have begun to speak of him with an expression I recognise, the one used for a distant relative who is probably sinister but is known to be rich. A colleague at work asked, with studied casualness, whether Gerald was "a dog or a partner," and seemed unsatisfied by my answer, which was "Both."

Gerald, for his part, has become a social figure. He has spawned offspring: little jars, distributed to neighbours, colleagues and a bewildered man at the garage, each bearing a handwritten label and a note of advice, which I have copied almost word for word from Priscilla. "He's very low-maintenance," I say, as I hand them over, and I watch their faces light up with the same gullible radiance, and feel, I am ashamed to say, a small, dark thrill. I understand now that this is how the thing spreads. It is not so much a hobby as a chain letter in edible form.

My wife has taken a rather philosophical view. On the whole, she is tolerant, as she has been of my fishing phase and my brief enthusiasm for the ukulele. But last week, as I was kneading dough at midnight, she appeared in the kitchen in her dressing gown, regarded the flour-dusted scene and observed, in a tone of deep thoughtfulness, that she had always imagined she would lose her husband to another woman, or perhaps to a motorbike. "I did not think," she said, "that it would be to a fungus."

I have defended myself with the argument that Gerald is not a fungus but a symbiotic community, an intricate and cooperative society, far more harmonious than most of the committees to which I have belonged. This did not move her. She has, however, begun to refer to herself, with a sigh, as "the other woman's husband's wife," which strikes me as a considerable step towards acceptance.

And so it goes. Gerald is now a year old, and in the best of health. He has survived a heatwave, two power cuts, a fortnight in the fridge while we were on holiday and a misguided attempt to feed him rye flour. I have asked myself, in quiet moments, what will happen when I am gone. I have decided to leave him in my will, to Priscilla, with a note. It will say, simply: "He's very low-maintenance."

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Короткий расслабленный гласный в центре рта; не русское «о» и не «а», губы не округляются.
Дифтонг: начните с широкого «а» и плавно уходите к «и»; второй элемент короткий и слабый.
Тёмный l: кончик языка упирается в дёсны, задняя часть оттянута назад; не смягчайте, как русское «ль».
Задняя часть языка касается мягкого нёба, воздух идёт через нос; не добавляйте отдельное «г».

questions.question: Who gave Gerald to the narrator?
What is Gerald?
questions.answer: A sourdough starter, a living culture of yeast and bacteria.

questions.question: What did the narrator do with Gerald when visiting his mother-in-law?
questions.answer: He took Gerald with him in a jar on the back seat.

questions.question: What does the narrator plan to do with Gerald in his will?
questions.answer: Leave him to Priscilla with a note.
